findings.headline: Property fund portfolio carrying £2.85m (16.81%) cumulative loss on £16.99m invested since 2016-18
findings.detail: The council holds property fund units purchased 2016-2018 with original cost of £16,989,766 and current net asset value of £14,138,540. Cumulative loss is £2,851,226. Largest losses are Schroder (-27.16%), AEW (-21.67%), BlackRock (-10.35%), and Threadneedle (-12.24%). Only M&G is liquidating and has returned a gain of £124,317. Fair value movements are reversed through reserves each year-end. Q1 quarterly movement showed a further £172,951 decrease in NAV.
findings.matters: The council has deployed substantial capital into property-backed investments at a poor point in the market cycle; whilst fair-value losses are reversed through reserves, the underlying capital allocation reflects poor judgment and ongoing exposure to further potential decline
findings.figures: Total invested: £16,989,766; current NAV: £14,138,540; cumulative loss: £2,851,226 (16.81%); Q1 decrease: £172,951; M&G distributions received: £4,124,317 on £4m (gain £124,317)
findings.quote: The Council purchased property fund units between 2016 and 2018. The overall change in the combined Net Asset Values for all funds during the first quarter of 2026/27 has been a decrease of £172,951

findings.headline: Council plans to borrow £3m from October 2026, nearly quadrupling its debt from £1m
findings.detail: Boston currently has £1m of PWLB debt (4.81%, maturing July 2030). The council has budgeted to take £3m of short-term borrowing from 1 October 2026 at an estimated rate of 3.50%. This would increase gross external debt from £1m to £4m. The quoted rate of 3.50% is notably below current PWLB certainty rates (5.98% on 30 June 2026), suggesting use of money market borrowing.
findings.matters: A tripling of debt from £1m to £4m is a material change to the council's financial risk profile and leverage position, even if short-term; clarity is needed on the source, duration, and purpose of this borrowing
findings.figures: Current debt: £1m PWLB at 4.81% (maturity 15 July 2030); planned new borrowing: £3m from 1 October 2026 at estimated 3.50%; forecast gross external debt: £4,000k
findings.quote: The Council has budgeted to take £3m of new short term borrowing from 1 October 2026 at an estimated rate of 3.50%

findings.headline: Investment income forecast to exceed budget by £647,511 (80%), but entirely dependent on temporary factors
findings.detail: The council's investment income forecast outturn is £1,453,491 against a budget of £805,980. The council has explicitly attributed this £647,511 favorable variance to two temporary conditions: (1) market interest rates being higher than the 2026/27 budget assumed, and (2) elevated cash balances resulting from capital programme slippage. Treasury investments achieved 4.45% return and property funds 3.80%.
findings.matters: This substantial outperformance (80% above budget) will reverse once capital spending resumes and rates fall; a lender must discount this from the council's sustainable financial position
findings.figures: Budget £805,980 vs forecast outturn £1,453,491; variance £647,511 favorable; rates achieved: treasury 4.45%, property funds 3.80%, combined 4.15%
findings.quote: The higher level of investment income achieved compared to the original budget is due to interest rates in the market being higher than the budgeted return for 2026/27 and balances available for investment being higher due to slippage in the 2025/26 capital programme

findings.headline: Capital programme severely underspent in Q1, with only 14% of annual budget delivered
findings.detail: Capital expenditure reached just £4,211k of a £30,596k budget in the quarter. The council explicitly identifies this underspend as creating backlogs of unspent funding. This follows noted slippage in the prior year (2025/26), suggesting the under-delivery may be structural rather than one-off.
findings.matters: A capital programme running at 14% of forecast pace through Q1 raises questions about the council's ability to deliver its strategic and service plans on schedule, and may indicate planning or resource constraints that require intervention
findings.figures: Capital expenditure: £4,211k Q1 actual vs £30,596k budget (13.8% delivery rate)
findings.quote: balances available for investment being higher due to slippage in the 2025/26 capital programme

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - skills audit survey - collective results
findings.headline: Half of audit committee members have only basic knowledge or no experience in Treasury Management
findings.detail: The audit identifies Treasury Management as a main development area, with ratings showing 17% of members report no experience and 33% report basic knowledge—totalling 50% with less than intermediate knowledge. Counter Fraud shows a similar pattern: 8% no experience, 42% basic knowledge.
findings.matters: A lender assessing council finances would want the audit committee overseeing borrowing, investments, and cash management to have strong Treasury Management knowledge. A knowledge gap here represents a constraint on oversight of decisions material to lending risk.
findings.quote: Treasury Management and Counter Fraud are the main areas for development, with around half of respondents reporting only basic knowledge or no experience.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - skills audit survey - collective results
findings.headline: Committee identifies that infrequent meetings compromise monitoring and decision-making effectiveness
findings.detail: Committee members report in Section 6 that infrequent meetings create large unwieldy agendas, which they directly link to ineffective monitoring and decision-making. This is the committee's own assessment of a structural limitation on its governance function.
findings.matters: A lender would want to know whether Boston's audit committee can effectively monitor financial management and compliance. The committee's own identification of meeting frequency as a constraint on monitoring effectiveness signals a governance risk.
findings.figures: none
findings.quote: Infrequent meetings lead to large cumbersome agendas, which in turn lead to ineffective monitoring and decision making

findings.headline: Staff retention risk elevated by LGR, with Workforce Development Strategy refresh targeted for 30 September 2026.
findings.detail: Staff retention and resilience is rated HIGH risk (score 12). The partnership is managing this through workforce development programmes and capacity reserves. A Workforce Development Strategy refresh is planned this year in light of LGR, targeting a reduction to MEDIUM risk (score 9) by 30 September 2026.
findings.matters: Staff retention directly affects service delivery and organisational stability. A council managing LGR while addressing staffing challenges faces compounded organisational risk.
findings.figures: Current risk score 12 (HIGH), target 30 September 2026, target score 9 (MEDIUM)
findings.quote: A refresh of the Workforce Development Strategy action plan will take place this year, in light of LGR, to help ensure colleagues have the skills and confidence required to continue to want to work in Local Government post re-organisation.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates prolonged organisational uncertainty with no expected risk reduction.
findings.detail: LGR is identified as creating a prolonged period of uncertainty affecting organisational culture, workforce stability, leadership capacity and change readiness, as well as service delivery and community confidence. Boston is awaiting the outcome of the LGR proposal. This is rated as HIGH risk (score 12) with no reduction expected (target remains score 12).
findings.matters: Organisational restructuring creates uncertainty that could affect financial performance, service continuity and leadership. A lender needs to understand LGR timing and likely outcomes.
findings.figures: Current risk score 12 (HIGH), target risk score 12 (HIGH)
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation will create a prolonged period of uncertainty impacting organisational culture, workforce stability, leadership capacity and change readiness, as well as service delivery and community confidence.

findings.headline: Boston Council faces funding gaps being addressed through partnership-based savings with a 30 September 2026 deadline to reduce risk from HIGH to MEDIUM.
findings.detail: Local Government funding challenges are described as inevitable and evidenced by partner funding gaps. The partnership is pursuing cost efficiencies and commercial opportunities identified in its business case. The funding risk is currently rated HIGH (score 16) with a formal target to reduce to MEDIUM (score 9) by 30 September 2026.
findings.matters: A lender must understand whether a council faces structural funding gaps and whether its mitigation strategy (partnership efficiencies) is credible and progressing to plan.
findings.figures: Current risk score 16 (HIGH), target 30 September 2026, target score 9 (MEDIUM)
findings.quote: Local Government funding challenges are inevitable and evidenced by each partner's funding gaps. The business case assumes a shared opportunity for efficient services and shared commercial opportunities and provides a significant opportunity to respond to this on-going challenge.

findings.headline: Risk appetite statements have not been formally adopted and will not be adopted until December 2026.
findings.detail: One of the seven high-priority audit findings is the absence of formal risk appetite statements. According to the audit response, drafts were signed off by Senior Leadership Team and scheduled for Cabinet adoption on 30 August 2026, but formal adoption has been pushed to December 2026.
findings.matters: Without documented risk appetite statements, the council's tolerance for different types of risk remains undefined, creating inconsistency in governance decisions and risk-taking.
findings.figures: Adoption scheduled December 2026; original presentation date was 30 August 2026
findings.quote: Absence of risk appetite statements. High. Adoption of risk appetite statements. December 2026. Drafts have been signed off by SLT. The Boston draft statement will be presented to Cabinet for adoption on 30th August as per the Risk Management Framework.

findings.headline: Three high-level risks have action deadlines of 30 September 2026, twelve days after this committee meeting.
findings.detail: Environment Act compliance (BBC12: H 16), Partnership Funding (SELCP-07: H 16), and Partnership Staffing (SELCP-08: H 12) all have action dates of 30/09/2026. The report notes that Environment Act and Partnership action dates were updated in Q1 to reflect project work timelines.
findings.matters: Multiple critical risk actions converging on the same date, shortly after this committee meeting, indicates compressed timelines for remediation of high-level risks.
findings.figures: 3 high-level risks due 30/09/2026; Environment Act and Partnership risks both H (16); Partnership Staffing H (12)
findings.quote: BBC12: Environment Act H (16) ↔ 30/09/2026. Q1 update: action date updated to reflect project work. SELCP-07: Funding H (16) ↔ 30/09/2026. Q1 update: action date updated. SELCP-08: Staffing H (12) ↔ 30/09/2026. Q1 update: action date updated

findings.headline: Budget risk rated high with no planned remedial action to move it to target level.
findings.detail: BBC05 (Budget) is scored at H (16), placing it in the high-risk category. The Action RAG column shows N/A, indicating no planned action is being taken to move this risk to its target level.
findings.matters: A high-impact budget risk without an active mitigation plan poses a direct threat to financial stability and places the council's spending under question.
findings.quote: BBC05: Budget H (16) ↔ N/A

findings.headline: Internal audit finds limited assurance in risk management with seven findings requiring remediation.
findings.detail: The auditors completed a SELCP Risk Management, Training, Awareness and Engagement audit and found limited assurance with seven findings: four rated high (absence of risk appetite statements, inconsistent reporting, gaps in Risk Management Framework, lack of formal training) and three rated medium. Several actions were reportedly already implemented in Q1, but risk appetite statements remain unadopted, with Cabinet adoption now scheduled for December 2026.
findings.matters: Limited assurance indicates weak controls in the council's governance and risk management framework, undermining the credibility of risk mitigation and decision-making.
findings.figures: 7 findings total; 4 high-priority; 3 medium-priority
findings.quote: The internal auditors have completed their SELCP Risk Management, Training, Awareness and Engagement audit. The outcome was limited assurance with 7 findings.

findings.headline: Council progressing Local Government Reorganisation programme through March 2027
findings.detail: One of the council's forward governance actions is to continue work towards Local Government Reorganisation with a proactive yet proportionate approach through April 2026 to March 2027. This represents a significant structural change that will affect the council's future governance arrangements and financial position.
findings.matters: Local government reorganisation involves substantial uncertainty about future structure, scope and financial position, creating a material risk factor that a lender must assess.
findings.figures: April 2026 to March 2027
findings.quote: Continue to work towards Local Government Reorganisation with a proactive yet proportionate approach.

findings.headline: Council undertook reviews of financial resilience and skills capacity, with actions embedding through 26/27
findings.detail: The council has carried out reviews of financial resilience including assessment of skills and management capacity. Actions arising from these reviews are being embedded throughout 2026/27, indicating the council identified gaps in its financial management capability that are now being addressed.
findings.matters: A council's financial management capacity—both systems and staff capability—is critical to sustainable financial management and effective response to budget pressures.
findings.figures: Actions embedding through 26/27
findings.quote: Monitoring of 'Financial Resilience including skills capacity and Management Code compliance'

findings.headline: Savings identification and monitoring received limited assurance in Q1 25/26, with revised approach now being embedded
findings.detail: The council's process for identifying and monitoring delivery of savings achieved limited assurance from internal audit in Q1, indicating initial deficiencies in tracking whether budgeted savings were materializing. A revised approach has been implemented and is now being embedded throughout the organization, with ongoing monitoring planned for 26/27.
findings.matters: A council that cannot reliably track whether its savings plans are being delivered loses visibility of its financial position and cannot respond effectively to budget pressures.
findings.figures: Limited assurance rating in Q1
findings.quote: Monitoring of 'Identification and Monitoring of savings' (due to limited assurance rating in Q1)

findings.headline: Internal audit identified AI governance gaps; council implementing recommendations through 2026/27.
findings.detail: Rapid adoption of AI across council services created governance and oversight gaps. Internal audit flagged Medium risk (score 9) with target Medium (6). Remediation underway through 2026/27 covering data privacy, compliance, service quality and public trust. Controls include AI Working Group, risk register, legal review, staff training and monitoring by IT and Information Governance teams.
findings.matters: A lender or audit committee assessing operational and reputational risk needs to know emerging AI governance gaps have been identified and are being actively remediated.
findings.figures: Current risk Medium (9); target Medium (6); implementation deadline 30/9/2026
findings.quote: Implementation of recommendations from internal audit ongoing in 26/27

findings.headline: Council establishes end-2026 start date for new local plan to meet 2029 government delivery deadline under reformed planning system.
findings.detail: New government planning regulations (March 2026) require councils to deliver new local plans within 30 months under reformed system, or face government intervention and loss of development control. South East Lincolnshire Local Plan (2019) is out of date. Boston faces High current risk (score 12) with target Medium (6). Mitigation includes appointment of specialist Local Plans project manager. Timeline 'now established for new plan - commencement by end of 2026' to meet 2029 deadline.
findings.matters: A lender assessing local economic growth prospects needs to know the council has visible local plan capacity and delivery timeline. Failure would restrict inward investment and development pipeline.
findings.figures: 30-month delivery timeline; commencement deadline end 2026; current risk High (12); target Medium (6)
findings.quote: Timeline now established for new plan - commencement by end of 2026

findings.headline: Waste depot capacity constraint resolved through secured extension and lease agreement.
findings.detail: St Johns Road depot faced insufficient capacity under waste operator licence for future housing growth and food waste vehicles. Council has secured depot extension with lease commencing 1 April 2025 and approved associated budgets. Risk downgraded to Minimal (2).
findings.matters: A lender tracking capital readiness and operational constraints needs confirmation this infrastructure limitation has been removed and funding secured.
findings.figures: Lease commencement 1 April 2025; risk score Minimal (2)
findings.quote: Extension and budgets required have been agreed

findings.headline: Government confirms £1.1 billion EPR scheme funding; Boston receives £946,000 for 2025/26.
findings.detail: Extended Producer Responsibility legislation transfers household waste collection funding from local taxpayers to product producers. Government has committed £1.1 billion nationally to mitigate council impact. Boston has received formal notification of £946,000 for 2025/26, providing confirmed budget settlement and reducing prior funding uncertainty for waste collection.
findings.matters: A lender tracking waste service funding sustainability and budget headroom needs confirmation this funding stream is secured, materially improving budget predictability.
findings.figures: £1.1 billion national guarantee; £946,000 Boston 2025/26 allocation
findings.quote: The government budget has provided a significant measure to reduce the risk around the introduction of the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) scheme by guaranteeing £1.1 billion in funding for local authorities. This assurance helps local councils plan their budgets effectively. BBC has received notification of payment for 2025/26 - £946,000

findings.headline: Environment Act waste service transformation faces ongoing revenue funding uncertainty despite initial New Burdens funding.
findings.detail: Compliance with Environment Act 2021 requires significant operational changes to waste services. The council has secured initial New Burdens funding but states that ongoing revenue funding is unclear. Current risk is High (16) with target Medium (9) by end September 2026. Mitigation includes depot extension (lease agreed April 2025), vehicle budgets approved, and establishment of Waste Improvement Programme Board reporting to Senior Leadership Team.
findings.matters: A finance director and potential lender need clarity on whether waste service compliance costs are sustainably funded, given mandatory nature of legislation and material budgetary impact.
findings.figures: Current risk High (16); target Medium (9); deadline 30/09/2026
findings.quote: although some New Burdens has been made available information is not provided on the ongoing New Burdens revenue funding to meet the additional cost of service delivery

findings.headline: Long-term budget balancing carries sustained high risk with no improvement trajectory planned.
findings.detail: The council faces High risk (score 16) on budget balancing due to government funding reductions, income decline, capital expenditure pressures, IDB levy impact, inflation and fuel costs. Both current and target risk scores remain at High (16), indicating no planned improvement. The council has implemented a Medium Term Financial Strategy, savings plan, and sound reserves but acknowledges ongoing uncertainty.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's structural deficit risk and medium-term financial sustainability needs to know the council sees endemic budget pressure without a recovery plan.
findings.figures: Current risk score High (16); target risk score High (16)
findings.quote: Risk around the long term balancing of the budget with economic and funding uncertainty

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit September 26 BBC Progress Report
findings.headline: HR Performance Management framework is not being applied consistently; appraisals, objective-setting and performance reviews are not always completed.
findings.detail: The HR Performance Management audit (Adequate rating) found that while a well-established performance management framework exists with clear policies and guidance, application is inconsistent across the partnership. Appraisals and objective setting are not always completed, with limited follow-up on overdue activity. Weaknesses were also identified in record-keeping and limited evidence linking performance reviews to training, workforce planning and organisational priorities.
findings.matters: Inconsistent application of HR performance management suggests either managerial compliance gaps or framework design issues; weak record-keeping and linking to workforce planning affects strategic workforce management.
findings.figures: Adequate assurance rating. One high, two medium, two low findings identified.
findings.quote: The audit identified that the framework is not being applied consistently across BBC. Appraisals, objective setting and performance reviews are not always completed, and there is limited evidence of effective follow-up where activity is overdue.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit September 26 BBC Progress Report
findings.headline: Payroll control environment depends on undocumented procedures and informal arrangements, creating resilience risk in event of staff turnover.
findings.detail: The Payroll audit (Adequate rating) found that while key controls operated effectively, there is heavy reliance on staff knowledge rather than formal documented procedures. Governance arrangements for outsourced payroll services are not sufficiently defined, particularly regarding supplier performance and backup/recovery controls. The audit concluded that documented procedures would enhance the control environment and reduce dependency on specific individuals.
findings.matters: Payroll processing is a critical control; undocumented reliance on individual staff knowledge creates operational and compliance risk if key personnel leave or are unavailable.
findings.figures: Adequate assurance rating; two medium findings identified. One finding was addressed before report finalisation.
findings.quote: reliance on staff knowledge rather than documented procedures, creating resilience risks in the event of staff turnover or absence. In addition, governance arrangements for obtaining assurance over outsourced payroll services, particularly in relation to supplier performance and backup and recovery controls, were not sufficiently defined.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit September 26 BBC Progress Report
findings.headline: Prior savings audit (Identification of Savings – 2nd Review, Limited assurance) has two management actions still requiring follow-up.
findings.detail: The 2024/25 Identification of Savings – 2nd Review audit reported Limited assurance and identified actions to address identified gaps. Of three management actions, one has been closed and two remain requiring follow-up, indicating that even at this stage of the financial year these actions have not been fully resolved.
findings.matters: Unresolved actions from a Limited assurance savings audit suggest identified savings delivery risks remain unmitigated.
findings.figures: Three management actions total; one closed; two requiring follow-up. Limited assurance opinion.
findings.quote: 2025/26 Identification of Savings - 2nd ReviewMar-26 S151 Officer Limited 3 1 0 2

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit September 26 BBC Progress Report
findings.headline: Financial Skills, Capacity & Management audit draft issued six months ago (March 2026) remains unresolved and awaiting management response in September 2026.
findings.detail: This audit contains four medium and one low findings relating to finance team capacity and capability. The draft has been outstanding since March with no indication of when management will respond or the final report will be issued. This audit is critical to understanding whether the council's finance function has adequate capacity and skills.
findings.matters: Finance team capacity directly affects the council's ability to manage its budget, forecasting, and financial reporting; unresolved audit findings suggest underlying gaps remain unaddressed.
findings.figures: Draft issued March 2026; four medium findings, one low finding; Adequate assurance rating despite 6-month delay on finalisation.
findings.quote: December 2025 (Draft issued March 2026) ... 4 Medium and 1 Low. Adequate

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit September 26 BBC Progress Report
findings.headline: Savings audit has not commenced despite being scheduled in the 2024/25 plan, nine months into the financial year.
findings.detail: The Savings: Accountability & Delivery audit (S151 Officer sponsor) shows no progress across any stage: scoping, audit objective definition, fieldwork, draft report, final report, or assurance opinion are all incomplete. With 50% of the audit plan completed mid-year, this audit remains in the half not yet started.
findings.matters: A council managing savings delivery has no audit visibility or assurance over whether planned savings are being realised or tracked.
findings.figures: 50% of the annual audit plan not yet commenced; Savings audit is one of four audits not started.
findings.quote: the internal audit plan is progressing as expected, with 50% of the plan completed mid-way through quarter two.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit September 26 BBC Progress Report
findings.headline: Risk management framework judged Limited assurance with governance and reporting failures; five actions from prior audit remain incomplete past their implementation dates.
findings.detail: The September 2026 risk management audit identified that risk appetite had not been formally established, risk reporting lacked consistency and clarity, and the framework was not fully defined. Critically, five management actions from the 2025 audit remain outstanding despite implementation dates of September 2025, January 2026, and March 2026. The audit identified four high and three medium findings requiring management action.
findings.matters: A council unable to establish, communicate and embed its risk management framework cannot reliably manage strategic and operational risks; delayed action remediation suggests execution problems.
findings.figures: Five actions overdue (September 2025, January 2026, March 2026). Four high findings, three medium findings from September 2026 audit.
findings.quote: Five actions agreed following the 2025 internal audit remain incomplete and have not been embedded, despite scheduled implementation dates of September 2025 (one action), January 2026 (three actions), and March 2026 (one action) which limited assurance that key control gaps were addressed.

findings.headline: M&G Property Fund liquidation generates £241,556 for capital financing; original investment was unfinanced
findings.detail: The council is liquidating its M&G Property Fund investment, realizing £241,556 in distributions to support MRP (capital repayment) funding. The original property fund investment was purchased without borrowing—funded instead from revenue or reserves—which is noteworthy for an asset-purchase decision.
findings.matters: This shows the council is actively managing its investment portfolio and redeploying capital proceeds. The decision to fund a property investment without borrowing and now liquidate it signals changes in investment strategy and capital financing approach.
findings.figures: M&G liquidation distribution £241,556
findings.quote: Liquidation Distributions (to be used for MRP Contributions as the original capital purchase was unfinanced)

findings.headline: Treasury investment income £169,389 ahead of Q1 budget; combined portfolio achieving 4.15% return
findings.detail: Treasury investments generated £222,301 gross interest in Q1 versus a budgeted £52,912, a favorable variance of £169,389. Combined returns across treasury and property fund holdings averaged 4.15%. The outperformance is driven by market interest rates running higher than the council's original budget assumptions.
findings.matters: Stronger-than-expected investment returns show effective cash management and improve the council's financial flexibility. The £647,521 forecast favorable variance for the full year is a material improvement to the financial position.
findings.figures: Treasury investments actual £222,301 vs budget £52,912 (£169,389 variance); combined investment return 4.15%; forecast full-year favorable variance £647,521
findings.quote: Treasury investments achieved an average rate of 4.45% and property fund investments achieved an estimated average rate of 3.80%. The combined rate achieved on all investments was 4.15%.

findings.headline: Capital programme slippage from 2025/26 is increasing cash available for investment
findings.detail: The council's investment balances are higher than budgeted in Q1 because capital spending from 2025/26 slipped into later years. This has left the council with more cash on hand than it expected to have at this point in the year, directly reducing its need to borrow.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether this is temporary slippage (spending will catch up later) or structural underspending. This directly affects the council's future borrowing requirements and capital finance profile.
findings.figures: Capital programme slippage identified as the driver of higher investment balances; Q1 overall net position shows £424,253 favorable variance against budget
findings.quote: balances available for investment being higher due to slippage in the capital programme from 2025/26

findings.headline: General Fund reserve set at £2m: described as prudent but low in absolute terms
findings.detail: The council holds a general fund reserve of £2.0m, which the Section 151 Officer describes as a prudent level. For a council of Boston's size (population 78,500, £12.3m revenue budget), this represents 1.8 months of operating expenditure. This is at the lower end of typical prudent reserves and leaves limited headroom for unexpected shocks.
findings.matters: A £2m reserve against a £12.3m budget provides limited financial buffer. Any material income shortfall or spending pressure cannot easily be absorbed. For a lender assessing financial stability, this indicates the council has little capacity to absorb adverse movements without needing to cut spending or breach its budget.
findings.figures: General Fund £2.0m (16% of net expenditure of £12.3m)
findings.quote: This reserve represents the Council's unallocated financial buffer. Its level is set at £2 million, as determined by the Section 151 Officer, reflecting a prudent position based on assessed risks, service pressures, and future uncertainties

findings.headline: Collection Fund deficits totalling £0.86m will reduce cash available to the council in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council tax collection fell £0.198m short of expected income; the business rates collection fell £0.662m short. These deficits will be shared with other preceptors (County Council, Police, Government) but the council bears its proportionate share, which reduces available cash in the next financial year. This is material for a council of this size.
findings.matters: Collection fund deficits constrain the council's revenue flexibility in the year following the shortfall. They reduce the cash available to deliver services or invest. For a lender, they signal whether the council's income forecasting is reliable and whether collection rates are weakening.
findings.figures: Council Tax Collection Fund deficit £0.198m; NNDR Collection Fund deficit £0.662m; total £0.860m
findings.quote: The balance on the Council Tax Collection Fund at 31 March 2026 showed a £0.198m deficit. This will be shared between the Borough, Lincolnshire County Council and Lincolnshire Police and Crime Commissioner in proportion with each authority's relative precept. The balance on the NNDR Collection Fund at 31 March 2026 showed a £0.662m deficit.

findings.headline: Capital programme significantly underspent: £17.1m (46%) of £37.4m budget unspent in 2025/26
findings.detail: The council's capital spending fell far short of plan, particularly on major regeneration schemes. Towns Fund projects delivered £7.2m of £14.8m (51% underspend); LUF projects £6.8m of £11.0m (38% underspend); BPF projects £3.7m of £7.6m (52% underspend). Boston Station project spent nothing against £0.864m budget; Haven Wharf zero against £2.8m. The council attributes this to projects remaining in progress and states funding will be carried forward.
findings.matters: A 46% capital budget variance suggests either weak project management, external blockers, or over-ambitious planning. This raises questions about delivery capacity and whether regeneration commitments can be executed. For a lender, it indicates execution risk on the council's forward plans.
findings.figures: Capital budget £37.4m, outturn £20.3m, underspend £17.1m (46%); Towns Fund £14.8m budget, £7.2m spent; LUF £11.0m budget, £6.8m spent; BPF £7.6m budget, £3.7m spent
findings.quote: The 2025/26 capital budget has not been fully utilised as a number of schemes remain in progress, the associated funding is therefore required to meet existing commitments and support the completion of projects within the Council's 2026/27 Capital Programme.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation underway with timeline extending through March 2027
findings.detail: The council is in the process of local government reorganisation, with work continuing through March 2027. This represents a significant structural change that will affect governance arrangements, staffing, and operational continuity.
findings.matters: Major organisational restructures create transition risk and can temporarily weaken controls and governance if not carefully managed; they also create uncertainty about future financial position and service continuity.
findings.figures: Timeline: April 2026 – March 2027
findings.quote: Continue to work towards Local Government Reorganisation with a proactive yet proportionate approach.

findings.headline: Council prioritizing improved timeliness of audit recommendation implementation as a governance priority
findings.detail: The council has identified as a key action to 'Improve the timeliness and effectiveness of implementing agreed audit actions by strengthening monitoring and accountability arrangements', with completion targeted for March 2027.
findings.matters: Delayed implementation of audit recommendations means governance weaknesses persist longer and issues are slower to resolve, extending periods of elevated risk.
findings.figures: Target completion March 2027
findings.quote: Improve the timeliness and effectiveness of implementing agreed audit actions by strengthening monitoring and accountability arrangements.

findings.headline: Audit of risk management framework identified improvements; further work required through 2026/27
findings.detail: An audit of the council's Risk Register in 2025 found it 'adequate' but identified several improvements that need to be implemented. The council explicitly states that further work is required in 2026/27 to implement these improvements.
findings.matters: An incomplete risk management framework means the council may not be systematically identifying and mitigating its financial and operational risks.
findings.figures: Audit completed 2025; further work required 2026/27
findings.quote: An audit of our Risk Register in 2025 provided adequate assurance and identified improvements to enhance the authority's risk management arrangements. Further work is required in 2026/27 to implement these improvements.

findings.headline: Council flagged for gaps in financial resilience and finance staff capacity
findings.detail: The council identified 'Financial Resilience including skills capacity and Management Code compliance' as a significant governance issue. Reviews have been undertaken but corrective actions are still 'being embedded through 26/27', suggesting the underlying capacity or capability issues have not been fully resolved.
findings.matters: Gaps in finance staffing or capability directly affect the quality of financial management, timeliness of reporting, and the risk of control failures.
findings.figures: Actions ongoing through 26/27
findings.quote: Monitoring of 'Financial Resilience including skills capacity and Management Code compliance'

findings.headline: Savings identification and monitoring received limited assurance in Q1 and remains ongoing into 2026/27
findings.detail: The council flagged 'Identification and Monitoring of savings' as a significant governance issue due to a limited assurance rating in Q1 25/26. A revised approach has been implemented but is explicitly marked 'Ongoing for 26/27', indicating it is not yet fully resolved and the council is still embedding the new process.
findings.matters: If a council cannot reliably identify whether planned savings are being delivered, it cannot effectively manage its budget or produce trustworthy financial forecasts.
findings.figures: Q1 25/26 limited assurance rating; ongoing through 26/27
findings.quote: Monitoring of 'Identification and Monitoring of savings' (due to limited assurance rating in Q1)

findings.headline: Audit recommendations are not implemented on schedule, with overdue management actions tracked through the year
findings.detail: Audit notes 'timely implementation of agreed actions remains an area for improvement, with progress reports continuing to track overdue management actions and follow-up activity.' This is a second-order risk: even when audit identifies a problem and management agrees a fix, the council is slow to execute it, leaving control gaps open longer than necessary.
findings.matters: Implementation delays on audit-agreed actions indicate either weak project management capability or insufficient management priority given to control remediation. Either signals difficulty in execution of other council priorities.
findings.figures: Overdue actions tracked 'throughout the year' in internal audit progress reports
findings.quote: internal audit reporting throughout the year has highlighted that the timely implementation of agreed actions remains an area for improvement, with progress reports continuing to track overdue management actions and follow-up activity.

findings.headline: Governance and control deficiencies in joint working arrangements with PSPS remain a recurring unresolved risk
findings.detail: Audit identifies a recurring multi-year pattern: 'in some key areas of joint working between the Council and PSPS, there is a lack of clarity and consistency in how services are governed and controlled. Audit work undertaken during 2025/26, has confirmed that this remains a key risk area requiring continued management focus.' This was confirmed through both insufficient controls and limited assurance reviews.
findings.matters: Persistent control gaps in partnership arrangements suggest the council lacks oversight of a material portion of its operations. If PSPS (Public Sector Partnership Services) arrangements are not properly governed, the council's financial obligations and risks may not be fully understood.
findings.figures: One 'Insufficient Controls' review and one 'Limited Assurance' review identified as demonstrating this pattern
findings.quote: in some key areas of joint working between the Council and PSPS, there is a lack of clarity and consistency in how services are governed and controlled. Audit work undertaken during 2025/26, has confirmed that this remains a key risk area requiring continued management focus.

findings.headline: Risk management framework is underdeveloped with no defined risk appetite and incomplete prior-year actions
findings.detail: Audit found 'key elements of risk management were underdeveloped, including the absence of a formally defined and operational risk appetite.' More concerning, 'Actions agreed following the 2025 internal audit remained incomplete and not embedded, despite past implementation dates, which limited assurance that key control gaps have been addressed.' The overall finding is that 'current arrangements do not provide confidence that risks are managed consistently and effectively.'
findings.matters: If the council cannot define and manage its own risks effectively, hidden control weaknesses or emerging liabilities could surface without warning. A lender needs to know the council's leadership can identify and respond to threats.
findings.figures: Risk management actions from 2025 'remained incomplete and not embedded, despite past implementation dates'
findings.quote: Actions agreed following the 2025 internal audit remained incomplete and not embedded, despite past implementation dates, which limited assurance that key control gaps have been addressed.

findings.headline: Council required emergency remedial work to close deficits in the 2026/27 budget after January 2026 scrutiny
findings.detail: Audit testing found that 'internal work had been completed to reduce potential deficits that were presented for scrutiny in two of the councils in January 2026.' This indicates the initial draft budget contained material deficits that had to be worked down before finalisation. The phrasing suggests this was reactive remediation rather than planned budget-setting.
findings.matters: A council that needs emergency deficit-closing work in budget scrutiny demonstrates weak financial planning and possible cash flow strain. Lenders depend on robust forward financial planning.
findings.figures: Deficits 'presented for scrutiny' in January 2026 required remediation before budget approval
findings.quote: Internal work had been completed to reduce potential deficits that were presented for scrutiny in two of the councils in January 2026.

findings.headline: Savings delivery for 2026/27 carries unproven residual financial risk due to newly implemented but untested governance process
findings.detail: Internal audit found insufficient controls over savings identification and monitoring in Q1, requiring immediate corrective action. By Q4, a new governance process had been implemented, but audit states there is 'currently limited assurance over the effectiveness and consistent embedding of the new methodology, and a residual financial risk remains over delivery of savings until it is fully tested.' Critically, there is no formal escalation process for savings proposals falling behind schedule.
findings.matters: Unproven savings delivery is a direct credit risk to lenders, particularly in the first year a new process is used. If the 2026/27 savings fail to materialise at the intended level, the council faces an immediate budget shortfall.
findings.figures: 2026/27 is the 'first year of the new process'; savings audit was unable to establish 'sufficient first or second-line controls' in Q1 with 'seven key findings' and 'five root causes identified'
findings.quote: As 2026/27 will be the first year of the new process, there is currently limited assurance over the effectiveness and consistent embedding of the new methodology, and a residual financial risk remains over delivery of savings until it is fully tested.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - BBC Draft Outturn Finance Capital Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Affordable Housing Commuted Sum spending blocked until properties are completed by third parties
findings.detail: £1.074m cannot be spent until properties are completed, per the draft funding agreement terms. This has forced the council to rephase the spending into 2027/28 and 2028/29, making delivery timeline dependent on external contractors completing construction on schedule.
findings.matters: Delivery and forecast risk: the council's spending is now hostage to third-party completion timelines; any construction delay creates cash-flow and budget variance
findings.figures: £1.074m rephased
findings.quote: Budget required to be rephased into 2027/28 and 2028/29. Draft funding agreement seeks completion of properties prior to payment.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - BBC Draft Outturn Finance Capital Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Haven Wharf project design changed from new-build to refurbishment, requiring subsidy control assessment
findings.detail: The £2.8m Haven Wharf project scope was amended from new construction to refurbishment of an existing building. Amendment has MHCLG agreement but is now pending completion of updated grant funding agreement and subsidy control assessment from external legal counsel (Freeths LLP). No spending has occurred despite the budget.
findings.matters: Material scope change affects value-for-money assessment and delivery risk; subsidy control requirement indicates regulatory complexity; zero spend to date creates delivery uncertainty
findings.figures: £2.8m budget, £0 outturn
findings.quote: Project design has been amended to be refurbishment of existing College building, rather than new build. Amendment agreed with MHCLG. Council letter of Intent issued to enable early pre-construction works pending completion of updated grant funding agreement and subsidy control assessment being undertaken by Freeths LLP.

findings.headline: Treasury investment income exceeded budget by £0.336m (19% outperformance)
findings.detail: The council's investment income outturn was £2.058m against a budgeted £1.722m, representing a favorable variance of £0.336m. This outperformance suggests better-than-expected returns on treasury management, though the paper does not specify whether this reflects higher interest rates, improved cash management, or increased investment base.
findings.matters: Income performance and stability matter to lenders; a 19% beat on treasury income could indicate sustainable improvements in cash management or temporary favorable conditions
findings.figures: Budget £1.722m; outturn £2.058m; variance £0.336m
findings.quote: The Council's 2025/26 budget for investment income is £1.722m, the draft outturn position is £2.058m, a favourable variance of £0.336m.

findings.headline: Capital programme underspent by £17.075m, rephased into future years
findings.detail: Against budgeted capital expenditure of £37.422m, the council spent £20.281m. Of the £17.141m underspend, £17.075m is attributed to rephasing of large capital projects into future years due to revised project timelines, described as normal for projects of this nature.
findings.matters: Material capital slippage affects forward delivery plans; lenders need to assess whether delays reflect routine project management or delivery capacity issues
findings.figures: Budget £37.422m; actual £20.281m; rephasing £17.075m
findings.quote: Due to the nature of capital projects, it is not uncommon for the timelines of large-scale projects to be revised. As a result, existing capital schemes totalling £17.075m of the £17.141m need to be rephased into future years.

findings.headline: Efficiency savings target of £1.429m has been delivered
findings.detail: The council set an efficiency target of £1.429m for the year. With the outturn showing a £0.064m underspend, the council concludes that the full savings target has been met.
findings.matters: Delivery of planned savings is essential for lender confidence in the council's budget discipline and financial planning reliability
findings.figures: £1.429m efficiency target
findings.quote: An efficiency target of £1.429m is included in the 2025/26 budget. Saving opportunities have been monitored throughout the year and in light of the outturn position showing an underspend of £0.064m it can be concluded that the savings target set, has been met.

findings.headline: Revenue position improved significantly through the year from forecasted £0.829m overspend to actual £0.064m underspend
findings.detail: Quarterly revenue forecasts showed progressive improvement: Q1 predicted £0.829m overspend, which reduced to £0.571m at Q2, £0.457m at Q3, and finally £0.064m underspend at year-end. This represents a £0.893m swing from initial forecast to actual position. The paper does not specify the causes of this improvement.
findings.matters: A large forecast-to-outturn variance indicates either significant budget forecasting issues or strong in-year cost control; lenders need to understand which
findings.figures: Q1 £0.829m overspend forecast, Q2 £0.571m, Q3 £0.457m, outturn £0.064m underspend
findings.quote: This represents a significant improvement from the forecast Q1 overspend at year end of £0.829m, reducing to £0.571m at Q2 and further to £0.457m at Q3.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - BBC Draft Outturn Finance Revenue Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council tax collection rate declined to 93.69% as cost-of-living crisis impacts payment
findings.detail: Council tax collection fell from 93.75% in 2024/25 to 93.69% in 2025/26. The council explicitly cited challenging collection conditions and the ongoing cost of living crisis as a factor, and continues to hold collection as a priority area requiring debt recovery efforts.
findings.matters: Declining collection rates directly reduce cash available to the council and may indicate deteriorating financial resilience among residents.
findings.figures: 93.69% collection rate (2025/26) vs 93.75% (2024/25); collectable debit £46.400m
findings.quote: Collection and recovery remained challenging in 2025/26 with the ongoing cost of living crisis being a factor.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - BBC Draft Outturn Finance Revenue Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Cremation services income miss by £0.140m, the largest single income underachievement
findings.detail: Cremation services, typically a predictable revenue stream, underachieved by £0.140m in 2025/26. This was the largest income shortfall identified, larger than combined underachievements in planning, building control, and markets.
findings.matters: Significant shortfall in a stable income stream raises questions about the council's income forecasting reliability across the portfolio.
findings.figures: £0.140m underachievement
findings.quote: the most notable underachievement's are; Cremation services by £0.140m

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - BBC Draft Outturn Finance Revenue Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Property fund investments are £2.832m below cost, with one fund liquidating
findings.detail: The council holds £14.157m in property fund investments valued £2.832m below purchase cost. The M&G fund is liquidating; it received £0.219m in distributions during 2025/26 and has only £0.117m book value remaining. Overall property fund valuations fell £0.589m during the year.
findings.matters: Material unrealised losses in the treasury portfolio indicate poor timing or selection of investments, and a liquidating fund suggests forced realisation of losses.
findings.figures: £14.157m fair value, £2.832m below cost, £0.589m valuation fall in-year, M&G book value £0.117m
findings.quote: As of 31 March 2026, the fair value of the remaining four funds was £14.157m which was £2.832m below the purchase cost.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4B - Treasury Management Strategy MRP Policy and AIS 2026-27
findings.headline: Rising precept payments requiring higher short-term cash reserves, signalling external budget pressure
findings.detail: Council increased its money market fund limit from £7.5m to £10m, explicitly stating this is 'due to the higher levels of cash required to be held short term to pay rising precept payments.' Precept obligations (police, fire, waste, etc.) are consuming a larger share of available liquidity.
findings.matters: Rising precept requirements reduce the council's discretionary use of cash and may indicate external pressures cascading from national bodies. Combined with declining reserves, this limits financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Money market fund limit: £7.5m → £10m; described as required for rising precept payments
findings.quote: increase in the maximum level of investments in individual money market funds from £7.5m to £10m. This is due to the higher levels of cash required to be held short term to pay rising precept payments

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4B - Treasury Management Strategy MRP Policy and AIS 2026-27
findings.headline: Council maintaining £22.3m under-borrowed position betting on interest rate falls that may not materialise
findings.detail: Despite a CFR of £26.3m, the council is only borrowing £4m, leaving £22.3m funded by cash and reserves. The strategy relies on treasury advisor forecasts that 5-year PWLB rates will fall from current 4.81% to 4.10% by Q4 2027. The strategy notes 'caution will be adopted with the 2026/27 treasury operations', indicating acknowledged risk.
findings.matters: If rates do not fall as forecast, the council will either be forced to borrow at higher rates later or continue drawing reserves. This is a material interest rate and liquidity risk.
findings.figures: Under-borrowing: £22,271k; current 5-year PWLB: 4.81%; forecast end-2027: 4.10%
findings.quote: This strategy is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels, albeit only once prevailing inflation concerns are addressed by restrictive near-term monetary policy

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4B - Treasury Management Strategy MRP Policy and AIS 2026-27
findings.headline: Cash position moves to negative expected investments in 2026/27, forcing reserve drawdown
findings.detail: Expected investment balances swing from £6.9m positive in 2025/26 to £2.1m negative in 2026/27 (and negative again in 2027/28, 2028/29, 2029/30). Negative balances mean the council will be drawing down reserves during the year to meet cash obligations.
findings.matters: Negative cash positions limit the council's ability to manage timing mismatches and reduce the buffer available for unexpected demands on cash.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4B - Treasury Management Strategy MRP Policy and AIS 2026-27
findings.headline: Core reserves falling 20% in one year to £18.2m, declining further to £15.4m by 2030/31
findings.detail: Total core funds forecast to drop from £22.7m (2025/26) to £18.2m (2026/27), then continue declining to £15.4m by 2030/31. This represents a 32% erosion of reserve balances over six years, with the largest drop in 2026/27. Key reserves including Capital Funding, Housing, and Neighbourhoods reserves all declining.
findings.matters: Reserves are the council's buffer against unexpected pressures or revenue shortfalls. A sustained 32% decline significantly reduces financial resilience and flexibility, a material credit concern.
findings.figures: Total Core Funds: £22,685k → £18,163k → £15,385k; Capital Funding reserve: £5,544k → £4,769k → £2,157k

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4B - Treasury Management Strategy MRP Policy and AIS 2026-27
findings.headline: Borrowing requirement jumps to £7.7m in 2026/27 from £700k in prior year, driven by capital programme timing
findings.detail: The capital financing requirement increases 40% from £18.9m to £26.3m. The borrowing requirement (unfunded capital) spikes from £700k to £7,726k. This reflects the completion of grant-funded programmes (Towns Fund, UKSPF, LUF, BPF projects ending 2027/28) and transition to permanent capital funding.
findings.matters: A sharp increase in borrowing requirement signals either unsustainable capital spending or material changes to the council's funding structure. A lender needs to understand whether this is temporary or structural.
findings.quote: Borrowing Requirement 700 7,726 1,293 979 100 100

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves declining from £16.2m to £11.8m over five years as council uses reserves to bridge budget gaps
findings.detail: The council's earmarked reserves are forecast to decline from £16,207k at 31 March 2026 to £11,821k by 31 March 2031—a depletion of £4,386k. This drawdown is driven by use of reserves to fund capital expenditure and to support the budget during the transition to delivering savings. The council explicitly describes this strategy: reserves will be used to provide 'a short-term mechanism to support delivery while longer-term savings are embedded.' Total reserves including general reserve decline from £18,482k to £14,464k.
findings.matters: A declining reserve position indicates the council is consuming accumulated savings and reducing its financial buffer. If savings targets are not met on schedule, the council could exhaust remaining reserves before achieving sustainable budget balance.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves: £16,207k (31 March 2026); £14,895k (31 March 2027); £11,821k (31 March 2031). Total reserves declining from £18,482k to £14,464k
findings.quote: Available reserve balances can be utilised to fund the efficiency targets, offering a short-term mechanism to support delivery while longer-term savings are embedded.

findings.headline: Efficiency savings of £1.49m to £1.87m annually are required from 2027/28 onwards with no detailed delivery plan disclosed
findings.detail: The council's 2026/27 budget is balanced with zero efficiency savings required. However, from 2027/28 onwards substantial unspecified efficiency targets are budgeted: £1,490k (2027/28), £1,709k (2028/29), £1,572k (2029/30), and £1,868k (2030/31). The document acknowledges these represent a significant challenge: 'The ongoing delivery of a significant level of efficiencies and savings is recognised as a key challenge to the Council that will require both political and cultural direction to ensure it is met.' Specific service areas, implementation plans, or sources of these savings are not detailed.
findings.matters: These are material unspecified savings targets. Failure to deliver them would create deficits in future years. The council's own characterisation of delivery as a 'key challenge requiring political and cultural direction' suggests execution risk and uncertainty about achievability.
findings.figures: Efficiency savings requirements: £1,490k (2027/28), £1,709k (2028/29), £1,572k (2029/30), £1,868k (2030/31). No savings required in 2026/27 (£0)
findings.quote: The ongoing delivery of a significant level of efficiencies and savings is recognised as a key challenge to the Council that will require both political and cultural direction to ensure it is met.

findings.headline: Business Rates system reset reduces retained income by £1.835m and dissolves the levy mitigation pool
findings.detail: From 1 April 2026, the Business Rates Retention System reset reduced the council's retained business rates income from £5,063k to £3,228k—a loss of £1,835k. Simultaneously, the Business Rates Pool Lincolnshire that previously mitigated the 50% levy on growth has been dissolved. The council had been paying levy contributions (£315k in 2025/26) within the pooling arrangement; from 2026/27 onwards any levy is due directly to central government. While the income reduction is compensated by increased Revenue Support Grant, the structural change removes the mitigation mechanism and shifts risk directly to the council.
findings.matters: This represents a fundamental change in the council's funding structure. The loss of pooled levy mitigation leaves the council exposed to the full 50% levy on any future business rates growth, increasing financial volatility and reducing downside protection.
findings.figures: Retained Business Rates income: £5,063k (2025/26) to £3,228k (2026/27); Levy payment to Lincolnshire Pool: £315k (2025/26) to £0 (2026/27 onwards)
findings.quote: The Business Rates Pool Lincolnshire will not continue into 2026/27; any levy payable on Business Rates growth will be due to Central Government.

findings.headline: Internal Drainage Board levies have escalated 52.57% in five years, with a further 4.96% increase budgeted for 2026/27
findings.detail: The council's total IDB levies rose from £2,013,712 in 2021/22 to £3,072,361 in 2026/27—a five-year increase of £1,058,649. The Witham Fourth IDB levy alone increased by £517,648 (46.72%) over the same period, now contributing £1,625,698 annually. The 2026/27 budget shows IDB costs rising by a further £145,311. The council identifies this as a 'substantial pressure' and has established a special interest group to lobby government on the issue.
findings.matters: IDB levies are non-discretionary, fixed costs the council cannot reduce or control. The document explicitly describes this as 'a recurring loss of revenue for the Council that grows with each passing year', making it a structural financial problem that compounds annually.
findings.quote: the embedded levy results in a recurring loss of revenue for the Council that grows with each passing year

findings.headline: Capital programme increasingly dependent on asset sales to generate capital receipts
findings.detail: Council notes forward availability of capital receipts is important to capital programme timing and scope. Council is actively marketing surplus assets to obtain receipts.
findings.matters: Reliance on asset sales to fund capital investment introduces timing and value uncertainty; indicates capital programme constrained by cash flow rather than priorities; realisation of asset values cannot be guaranteed.
findings.figures: Fixed assets valued at circa £41m; treasury holdings averaging £32m
findings.quote: The forward availability of capital receipts will play an important part in both the timing and scope of the capital programme. The Council is looking at ways of obtaining capital receipts through the active marketing of its surplus assets

findings.headline: Council holds limited levels of both general and specific reserves
findings.detail: Council explicitly states it maintains limited reserve levels, reducing its buffer to absorb unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls.
findings.matters: Limited reserves increase vulnerability to unexpected shocks or income variability; they reduce flexibility in responding to emerging challenges and indicate limited headroom for debt servicing.
findings.figures: No quantum disclosed; reserves described as 'limited'
findings.quote: Boston Borough Council holds limited levels of both general and specific reserves.

findings.headline: Business rates income flagged as significantly higher risk due to government policy changes
findings.detail: Council identifies changes to localised business rate retention system and recent government policy changes as creating yield uncertainty. Council explicitly states this income stream now carries significantly higher risk.
findings.matters: Business rates are a major revenue source; policy-driven uncertainty makes forecasting unreliable and could force additional service cuts or borrowing if yield declines.
findings.figures: Business rate yield subject to government policy changes and economic impacts
findings.quote: particularly as a result of economic impacts and recent changes in Government policy so this income stream has a significantly higher level of risk.

findings.headline: Council planning to use capital and treasury activities to relieve revenue budget pressure, worsening as interest rates rise
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly states the council will look to capital and treasury activities to help manage revenue shortfalls. Council acknowledges this approach will become more difficult as interest rates increase.
findings.matters: Using capital spending or treasury activity to solve revenue deficits is an unusual approach; rising interest costs will compound the revenue pressure and reduce capacity to service new borrowing.
findings.figures: Interest rates expected to increase; strategy period 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.quote: The Council will look towards its capital and treasury activities to mitigate and contribute to wards relieving pressure on its future revenue budgets particularly as interest rates increase.

findings.headline: Revenue budget balancing is deteriorating year-on-year with no expectation of improvement through 2030-31
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that each year the ability to balance the budget is becoming more challenging, driven by inflation, changes in customer requirements, and post-COVID income reductions. Council signals no optimism for financial improvement.
findings.matters: Mounting annual budget pressure raises questions about the council's ability to service debt, maintain service levels, or respond to emergencies; lenders need to understand this deteriorating trajectory.
findings.figures: Budget pressures forecast through 2030/31
findings.quote: Each year the ability to balance the budget is becoming more challenging, with options ranging from becoming more efficient, raising additional income and/or reducing services.

findings.paper_title: Annual Budget Report 2026/27, Medium Term Financial Strategy, Capital Programme and Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Policy/Strategy, Annual Delivery Plan, Living Wage Supplement and Pay Policy Statement
findings.headline: The Financial Settlement reflects 'unprecedented level of change' to the local government finance system, introducing 4 new consolidated grants and rolling 16 funding streams into RSG, creating operational complexity.
findings.detail: The 2025 Budget and Spending Review, 2024 Autumn Budget, and 20 November Policy Statement combined to produce what the report calls 'an unprecedented level of change to the Local Government Finance system and significant added complexity.' Four new consolidated grants were introduced, bringing together 16 funding streams; Boston is affected by 2 of these (Homelessness, Rough Sleeping & Domestic Abuse Grant and Crisis & Resilience Fund). The spending comparison basis changed from 2025/26 to 2024/25.
findings.matters: Rapid structural changes to funding mechanisms increase forecasting difficulty and create operational risk. Lenders need stable, predictable revenue bases; multiple simultaneous reforms reduce confidence in medium-term projections.
findings.figures: 4 new consolidated grants introduced; 2 applicable to Boston; spending comparisons assessed against 2024/25 values (not 2025/26).
findings.quote: the 2024 Autumn Budget & Spending Review, 2025 Budget and 20 November Policy Statement which collectively results in an unprecedented level of change to the Local Government Finance system and significant added complexity.

findings.paper_title: Annual Budget Report 2026/27, Medium Term Financial Strategy, Capital Programme and Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Policy/Strategy, Annual Delivery Plan, Living Wage Supplement and Pay Policy Statement
findings.headline: The Fair Funding Review introduces a 2-tier funding floor system where protection varies depending on how far each authority is from its 'newly assessed level of funding,' and Boston may not be receiving the highest tier.
findings.detail: MHCLG implemented a 2-tier funding floor system as part of the Fair Funding Review, with 'some Local Authorities' receiving different levels of protection depending on their distance from newly assessed funding levels. The document does not explicitly state which tier Boston occupies, but the language suggests variation in protection.
findings.matters: If Boston is in the lower tier of the funding floor, it has less protection against further funding reductions in future years. This affects medium-term financial stability and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: 2-tier system implemented; provisional allocations for 2027/28 and 2028/29 included in settlement.
findings.quote: MHCLG has decided to implement a 2-tier system of funding floors. This means that some Local Authorities will receive varying levels of funding protection depending on how far from the newly assessed level of funding they are.

findings.paper_title: Annual Budget Report 2026/27, Medium Term Financial Strategy, Capital Programme and Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Policy/Strategy, Annual Delivery Plan, Living Wage Supplement and Pay Policy Statement
findings.headline: Business Rates Retention System reset has reduced net retained income significantly and created uncertainty through revaluation, new multipliers, and appeals that can be backdated.
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review resets the system effective 1 April 2026, introducing 5 new multipliers in place of 2. The council lost £2.382m in S31 grants relating to business rates (rolled into higher Revenue Support Grant instead). The revaluation and multiplier changes create 'large amount of uncertainty,' and appeals against rateable values can be backdated, making 'estimating income accurately extremely challenging and potentially volatile.'
findings.matters: Business rates are volatile income streams for councils. A structural reset combined with revaluation and the risk of backdated appeals creates estimation risk and potential income shortfalls that could emerge during the budget year.
findings.figures: S31 Grants relating to Business Rates: £2.382m in 2025/26 → £0 in 2026/27; Business Rates income 2025/26 £2.830m vs 2026/27 £2.797m (net reduction of £33k after reset adjustments).
findings.quote: This coupled with uncertainties relating to appeals against rateable values for business premises, with the potential for successful appeals being backdated makes estimating income accurately extremely challenging and potentially volatile.

findings.paper_title: Annual Budget Report 2026/27, Medium Term Financial Strategy, Capital Programme and Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Policy/Strategy, Annual Delivery Plan, Living Wage Supplement and Pay Policy Statement
findings.headline: Internal Drainage Board levies are growing at 5% per year and have risen 47–61% since 2021/22, embedded in the council tax bill and beyond the council's control.
findings.detail: The council pays IDB costs totalling £3.072m in 2026/27, up from £2.927m the prior year (4.96% increase). Over five years from 2021/22, they have grown 52.57% (from £2.013m). Witham Fourth IDB alone is up 46.72%, Black Sluice 61.05%. The council states it is lobbying government and working with the boards to limit increases, but the levy is 'embedded' and the impact 'has an impact every year that passes.'
findings.matters: This is a recurring cost built into every council tax bill that grows faster than inflation and is beyond the council's control. For lenders, it signals a structural deterioration in the council's discretionary financial headroom.
findings.figures: IDB costs: £2.013m (2021/22) → £2.927m (2025/26) → £3.072m (2026/27); 52.57% growth over 5 years; Witham Fourth 46.72% over 5 years, Black Sluice 61.05%.
findings.quote: The Council is liaising with the local Internal Drainage Boards to work towards limiting future increases where possible. Lobbying of government is also underway with the impact of this loss of revenue to the Council due to the embedded levy having an impact every year that passes.

findings.headline: Possible Local Government Reorganisation in Lincolnshire creates strategic uncertainty with unquantified medium-term implications
findings.detail: The Council states: 'In the medium term, the implications for the Council as a result of the possible Local Government Reorganisation in Lincolnshire remains uncertain.' No timeline, probability, or financial scenario analysis is provided. This is a significant strategic uncertainty that could affect the council's structure, staffing, functions, and funding.
findings.matters: Unresolved structural reorganisation creates strategic uncertainty; lenders and finance directors cannot reliably forecast the council's medium-term trajectory or financial stability if reorganisation occurs.
findings.figures: No financial impact quantified
findings.quote: In the medium term, the implications for the Council as a result of the possible Local Government Reorganisation in Lincolnshire remains uncertain.

findings.headline: Internal Drainage Board pressures addressed through one-off funding and new transformation board, indicating structural cost issue
findings.detail: The Council reports 'pressures arising from Internal Drainage Board requirements, for which we have already received initial one-off funding.' In response, it has 'established an Innovation, Transformation, and Efficiency Board' to 'oversee efficiency targets and lead projects' to manage these pressures. One-off funding masks a structural cost problem; the new transformation board suggests these pressures are ongoing and require permanent solutions.
findings.matters: One-off funding for recurring cost pressures indicates the Council is using temporary fixes for structural problems; this is unsustainable and suggests budget pressures are larger than headline figures suggest.
findings.figures: One-off funding received for IDB requirements (amount not disclosed)
findings.quote: In response to pressures arising from Internal Drainage Board requirements, for which we have already received initial one-off funding, we have established an Innovation, Transformation, and Efficiency Board.

findings.headline: Combined £1.22m collection fund deficits will reduce funding to the council and other precepting authorities
findings.detail: The Council Tax Collection Fund showed an £886k deficit and the Business Rates Collection Fund a £334k deficit at year-end (31 March 2025). These deficits must be shared: the Council Tax deficit is split between Boston, Lincolnshire County Council, and the Police Authority; the NNDR deficit is split between Boston, the County Council, and Government. This indicates variance between budgeted and actual tax collection, reducing available revenue.
findings.matters: Collection fund deficits reduce the council's own revenue in the following year; they signal tax collection assumptions were optimistic and/or economic conditions are weaker than forecast.
findings.figures: Council Tax Collection Fund deficit: £886k; NNDR Collection Fund deficit: £334k; combined: £1.22m
findings.quote: The balance on the Council Tax Collection Fund at 31 March 2025 showed an £886k deficit. This will be shared between the Borough, Lincolnshire County Council and Lincolnshire Police and Crime Commissioner in proportion with each authority's relative precept.

findings.headline: £5.7m capital programme underspend signals project delivery issues across major regeneration schemes
findings.detail: Boston budgeted £20.814m in capital expenditure for 2024/25 but delivered only £15.070m (27% underspend). Major strategic schemes are affected: Towns Fund projects £2.1m underspent, BPF projects £2.6m underspent, and LUF projects £324k underspent. The Council states projects are 'still in progress' but this level of slippage across multiple funded schemes—including the Towns Fund Mayflower project (£1.083m underspent) and Boston Station (£864k underspent)—indicates persistent delivery challenges.
findings.matters: Capital programme slippage delays economic regeneration benefits and community investment; heavy reliance on external funding (Towns Fund, LUF, BPF) means delays cascade across financial years and test funder confidence in project execution.
findings.figures: Capital budget £20.814m, outturn £15.070m, variance £5.744m underspent; Towns Fund £10.623m budgeted, £8.514m spent (£2.109m under); BPF £4.488m budgeted, £1.906m spent (£2.582m under)
findings.quote: The 2024/25 capital budget has not been fully utilised as these projects are still in progress and therefore, the budgets are required for commitments to complete the programmes outlined in the Council's Capital Programme 2024/25.

findings.headline: Capital programme shows significant slippage (£24.4m carried forward from 2023/24) with sharp drop-off in 2025-26 to £5.2m
findings.detail: The 2024-25 capital programme of £32.6m includes £24.4m slippage from the prior year. The 2025-26 capital programme drops to £5.2m, assuming no further slippage. This suggests delivery challenges or funding uncertainty.
findings.matters: Large capital slippages indicate either scheme delays, planning/delivery issues, or funding uncertainty. The sharp drop in 2025-26 suggests capital investment may be contracting due to funding constraints.
findings.figures: 2024-25 capital programme: £32.6m (includes £24.4m slippage); 2025-26: £5.2m (assuming no slippage)
findings.quote: The Council's capital programme for the year is £32.6m (including slippage of £24.4m from 2023/24). The capital programme reduces to £5.2m in 2025-26 assuming there is no slippage from 2024-25.

findings.headline: Business rates collection rate at 93.8%, below national average; auditor attributes to pandemic impact and cost-of-living pressures
findings.detail: The council is an outlier in the LGA value-for-money benchmarking on business rates collection, with a net collection rate of 93.8% — below the mean for English district councils and consistent with the prior year. The auditor noted 2024-25 remained challenging with ongoing pandemic effects and cost-of-living pressures affecting recovery.
findings.matters: A 6.2% collection shortfall on business rates revenue is a material income loss in a council with tight savings margins. If economic pressures persist, collection recovery may be slow, creating further income volatility.
findings.figures: Net business rates collection rate 93.8%; below mean for English district councils; unchanged from prior year
findings.quote: The net collection rate was reported to Cabinet in the quarter four outturn report in July 2025 and showed a net collection rates for business rates of 93.8% which remained consistent from the prior year. The report noted that 2024-25 remained challenging with the long-term effect on collection and recovery as a result of the ongoing impact of the pandemic, and the cost-of-living challenges.

findings.headline: Net service spend per head rising significantly faster than national average; up 24% in one year from £40m to £48m gross expenditure
findings.detail: The council's total net service spend per head started as the lowest of peer councils in 2018/19 but has now risen faster than the national mean and is now above the mean for district councils.
